_comment: Single source of truth for every trained MLP variant, loaded and resolved by scripts/mlp_variants.py. JSON has no comment syntax, so '_'-prefixed keys are notes only, ignored by the loader. 'class_groups_base' must be 'CLASS_GROUPS' (original 6-class taxonomy) or 'MLP_CLASS_GROUPS' (standing 5-class, bus merged into large_vehicle) - both are resolved against the real dicts in dataloader.py, never duplicated here, so the taxonomy mapping itself always has exactly one source of truth. 'class_groups_overrides' (optional) merges on top of that base for a variant that needs one class to diverge, e.g. truck_separate. 'output_dir' is relative to MLP_DIR (results/mlp/); null means MLP_DIR itself, the standing baseline. 'features'/'extra_features' (optional) override mlp_classifier.py's own feature-set defaults. 'run_kwargs' (optional) overrides its hyperparameter defaults (epochs/batch_size/lr/hidden_dim).

baseline._note: Current working model: bus merged into large_vehicle, Design_Decisions.md decision 1's final resolution. Lives at MLP_DIR, mlp_classifier.py's own default.

bus_separate._note: Original, pre-merge taxonomy (bus kept separate). Kept for reference/comparison, not the standing model anymore.

epochs_1000._note: Ablation that informed the merge decision (MLP_Decisions_and_Findings.md section 2): 1000 epochs instead of 50, no meaningful gain past ~150-200.

truck_separate._note: Ablation that informed the merge decision (section 4): un-merges truck too, confirms decision 1's truck merge was correct.

bs32._note: Re-checks BATCH_SIZE=128 now that bus is merged: two_wheeler (7.0%) only needs bs=32, unlike bus's original 1.9%. Found no real difference (macro F1 0.687 vs baseline's 0.686) - not yet written up in MLP_Decisions_and_Findings.md, section 1's batch-size decision is still backed only by the miss-probability argument, not this empirical check.

range_sc._note: Swaps the feature set: range_sc binned like the other point-level features, in place of doppler_spread appended unbinned. Looked better, confirmed noise (section 5).

hidden8._note: Capacity ablation (section 6): HIDDEN_DIM=8 vs standing 16. No effect, even per-class.

hidden32._note: Capacity ablation (section 6): HIDDEN_DIM=32 vs standing 16. No effect, even per-class.

hidden64._note: Capacity ablation (section 6): HIDDEN_DIM=64 vs standing 16. No effect, even per-class.

deep10._note: Depth ablation (section 7): 10 hidden layers instead of 2, same HIDDEN_DIM=16, N_BINS=16 unchanged. First attempt (n_hidden_layers=10, dropout=0.3, no batch_norm, lr=1e-5) collapsed to predicting only the majority class - vanishing gradient through 10 unnormalized layers plus compounding dropout. Fixed by adding batch_norm=True, easing dropout to 0.1, raising lr to 1e-3. BatchNorm adds real per-epoch cost (25.3s/epoch vs 13.2s unnormalized), so epochs capped at 100 (~42min) to stay under the 45min budget - val accuracy plateaus around epoch 20-25 in a timing probe, so 100 leaves real margin past convergence.

n_points._note: Feature design test (section 8): baseline plus one extra scalar, n_points (instance's raw point count, appended unbinned like doppler_spread). The histogram features are fraction-of-points-per-bin, which throws point count away entirely - targets the pedestrian/pedestrian_group confusion (high pedestrian recall, low precision) directly, since that's fundamentally a 'how many people' question a fraction-normalized histogram can't answer.

raw_counts._note: Feature design test (section 8): same as baseline, but the histogram bins hold raw per-bin point counts instead of fractions (normalize=false). Fractions divide by total point count, which is exactly what makes n_points unrecoverable; raw counts embed it back in implicitly (a feature's bins sum to that instance's n_points) without adding a separate scalar. Tradeoff: sparse and busy instances now live on different numeric scales for the same underlying shape.

spatial_extent._note: Feature design test (section 9): drops x_rel/y_rel (per-point, orientation-dependent - a car seen broadside vs head-on spreads very differently across the two axes for the same physical object) in favor of spatial_extent, one orientation-robust scalar per instance (bounding-box diagonal, sqrt(x_extent^2+y_extent^2)), appended unbinned like doppler_spread. Same underlying concept (how big/spread-out is this instance's footprint), independent of aspect angle.

azimuth_extent._note: Feature design test (section 9): baseline plus one extra scalar, azimuth_extent (instance's angular spread as seen by the sensor, max-min of azimuth_sc). Different physical quantity than spatial_extent: a fixed-size object further away subtends a smaller angle, so this folds in range-dependent apparent size rather than raw Euclidean spread. azimuth_sc was untried until now, every other point-level column (rcs, vr, vr_compensated, x_cc, y_cc, range_sc) already had a feature built from it.

stat_descriptors._note: Feature design test (section 11): replaces the 65-dim histogram encoding entirely with 8 explicit per-instance statistics. rcs gets mean/median/std (mean/median for central tendency - car's f1=0.839 at n=1 comes almost entirely from the raw RCS value, a std-only encoding would lose that; std because unlike vr_compensated there's no existing rcs-spread feature, so no redundancy risk, and a rigid multi-reflector object like a car plausibly has higher point-to-point RCS variance than a soft scatterer like a pedestrian). vr_compensated gets mean/median only, std deliberately omitted since doppler_spread (MAD of vr_compensated, already in the feature set) already covers that ground. radial (new: sqrt(x_rel^2+y_rel^2), per-point Euclidean distance from the instance's own centroid) gets std, exactly rotation-invariant (trace of the instance's 2D covariance matrix), unlike x_rel/y_rel individually. azimuth_sc gets std (a softer version of azimuth_extent). doppler_spread appended as-is, unbinned. Raw azimuth mean/median and the min/max ratio were both considered and dropped: azimuth's absolute position is scene-geometry, not object physics (risk of a dataset-collection artifact rather than a real class signal); min/max is undefined (0/0) for 34% of x_rel/y_rel instances and sign-flips for 32-66% of the rest, worse than dividing by a small number, dividing by literally zero on a third of the data.

gaussian_range._note: Feature design test (section 12): otherwise identical to baseline, only the bin range formula changes. Bins are still equal-width and fraction-normalized (16 bins), but the outer range each feature is split across comes from [mean-2std, mean+2std] (histogram_separability.fit_bin_edges's range_method='gaussian') instead of decision 2's [1st, 99th] percentile. The two ranges agree for a roughly normal distribution but diverge for a skewed/heavy-tailed one, which is what RCS/Doppler look like here - and unlike most feature-design tests in this project, bin range affects every instance including n=1, not just ones with enough points to aggregate.

quantile_bins._note: Feature design test (section 12, alongside gaussian_range): otherwise identical to baseline, but bins are no longer equal-width. Edges are placed so each bin holds roughly the same fraction of training points (histogram_separability.fit_bin_edges's range_method='quantile'), giving more resolution where a feature's data is actually dense and less where it's sparse, instead of 16 bins spent uniformly across the range regardless of where the points are. A stronger version of the same idea gaussian_range tested (which only changed the outer clipping range, still equal-width inside it) and gaussian_range landed null.

standardized._note: Feature design test: otherwise identical to baseline, z-score standardizes doppler_spread (train-fit mean/std, applied unchanged to val/test) before it reaches the network. The 64 histogram-bin columns are already bounded [0,1] (fractions); doppler_spread isn't (train range 0-59.2, mean 0.233), a scale mismatch at the input layer flagged in section 7's deep10 writeup but not tested there. Result: macro F1 0.688 vs baseline's 0.686, inside the noise floor - not yet written up in MLP_Decisions_and_Findings.md, so section 7's 'open, not acted on' note is currently stale (this was run, just not incorporated into the doc).

combined_features._note: Final feature-design test before tagging v1.0: baseline's histograms plus every other feature tried across sections 5-13, added, not replacing anything. Histograms (16 bins each): rcs, vr_compensated, x_rel, y_rel (baseline's 4) plus range_sc, azimuth_sc (new). Unbinned scalars: doppler_spread (baseline's 1) plus n_points, azimuth_extent, spatial_extent, rcs_extent, range_extent (rcs_extent/range_extent new, same max-min-per-instance recipe as azimuth_extent). 102 dims total vs baseline's 65. Purely additive so it can't lose any signal baseline had; the question is whether stacking every previously-null-on-its-own feature together surfaces an interaction none of them showed individually. Expectation, going in: unlikely, per stat_descriptors (section 11) already combining a similar breadth of ideas and landing worse, not better, and the diagnosed ceiling (section 10, sparsity) isn't representational. If null, discard rather than write up.

rcs_extent_only._note: Follow-up to combined_features's zero-out importance check (section 14a): rcs_extent alone was the second-most load-bearing addition (-0.045 macro F1 when zeroed) and had never been tested standalone before. Isolates it: baseline's own 4 histograms unchanged, extra_features adds only rcs_extent (max-min of rcs per instance) alongside doppler_spread. Tests whether this one feature alone reproduces a meaningful slice of combined_features's gain.

spatial_extent_added._note: Follow-up to combined_features's zero-out importance check (section 14a): spatial_extent was the single most load-bearing addition (-0.080 macro F1 when zeroed), but section 9 only ever tested it as a replacement for x_rel/y_rel (null there, macro F1 0.690). This tests it as an addition instead: baseline's x_rel/y_rel histograms kept, spatial_extent appended alongside doppler_spread rather than swapped in for anything.
